Sanika’s intro carousel

Marker-pen annotation, straight onto the photograph — fat headers, circled titles, drawn arrows and dash bullets, the way you’d write on a printed picture. Eleven slides, one per photo, with the ink colour switching by slide and no wash sitting between the words and the image.

Posting notes

Small things that make a measurable difference.

Ratio
Keep it at 4:5. It’s the tallest ratio Instagram allows, so it takes up the most feed space — don’t let the uploader crop to square.
Cover
Slide 1. It’s the only one that has to stop a scroll.
Pin it
Pin the post to the top of your profile so it stays the first thing new visitors see.
Eleven is long
Instagram allows 20, but most people stop swiping around six. Slides 1–6 carry the whole introduction on their own — if you want a shorter cut, drop 7–10 and keep 11 as the closer.
The outline I couldn’t draw
The inspo traces a white cutout outline around the subject on several slides. That needs the figure separated from its background, which code can’t do reliably — but it’s two minutes a slide by hand: select the subject in Canva or Procreate, add an 8–12px white stroke, nudge it slightly. Slides 1, 5 and 11 are the ones worth doing.
Every photo is in
All eleven pictures you’ve sent have a slide. Nothing held back this time.

Built as eleven self-contained HTML slides. Three embedded faces do the handwriting — Permanent Marker for the headers, Patrick Hand for the lists, Caveat for the script accents — and every circle, underline, arrow, hook, dash, star and heart is inline SVG drawn slightly wrong on purpose, so the ovals overshoot where they close. There is no wash between the words and the picture: legibility comes from a four-way text outline, white behind dark ink and black behind light ink, plus a directional veil only on the slides that genuinely need one. The grade is deliberately light — the inspo’s photos aren’t filtered, so these get only a nudge of exposure for the dim interiors. Source and build scripts are in instagram/intro-carousel/.
